name: Esther
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: This story took place when Ahasuerus was king. His empire stretched from India all the way to Cush, with 127 provinces under his rule.{a}
Back then, King Ahasuerus ruled from his royal throne in the fortress city of Susa.{b}

When he had been king for three years, he threw a feast. He invited all his officials and servants. The commanders of the armies of Persia and Media came, along with the nobles and the rulers of the provinces.{c}
For a long time, 180 days in all, the king put his riches on display. He let everyone see the splendor of his kingdom and the glory of his greatness.{d}
When those days ended, a second feast began. This one was open to everyone in Susa’s fortress, great and small alike. For seven days it went on in the walled garden beside the king’s palace.

Curtains of white and blue cotton hung everywhere. Cords of fine white linen and purple cloth held them to silver rings set in marble pillars. On a floor of colored stones, marble, shell, and other costly stones stood gold and silver couches for the guests.{e}
Wine was poured into gold cups, and no two cups were alike. The king was generous, so there was plenty of royal wine.
The king had given an order about the drinking. No one had to drink more than he wanted. The servants were told to let every guest drink as much or as little as he liked.
Meanwhile, Queen Vashti gave a feast for the women in King Ahasuerus’s palace.{f}
On day seven, the wine had made the king merry. He sent for the seven officials who served him: Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas.{g}
“Bring Queen Vashti to me,” he said. “Have her wear her royal crown.” He meant to let the crowd of peoples and princes gaze at how beautiful she was, for her looks were stunning.{h}
The officials gave Queen Vashti the king’s order. But she would not come. At that, the king became furious. His anger blazed up like a fire inside him.
The king always talked with experts in law and justice. So he turned to his wise men, who understood the times, for advice.

The men closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan. These seven princes of Persia and Media had the right to come to the king at any time. No one in the kingdom ranked above them.
“What does the law say I must do to Queen Vashti?” the king asked. “She has disobeyed the order I sent her by my officials.”

Memucan answered, while the king and the princes listened. “The king is not the only one Queen Vashti has wronged,” he said. “She has wronged every prince and every person in every province of King Ahasuerus’s empire.

Every woman is going to hear about what the queen did. Then they will treat their husbands with scorn. ‘Remember Queen Vashti?’ they will say. ‘King Ahasuerus commanded her to appear before him, but she stayed away!’
This very day, the great ladies of Persia and Media will learn of it, and they will answer the king’s princes in the same way. Contempt and anger will spread everywhere.

So if the king agrees, let him send out a royal order. Put it among the laws of Persia and Media, which stand forever. It should say that Vashti may never again come into King Ahasuerus’s presence. Then let the king hand her royal place to another woman, one more worthy than she is.
When the king’s order is announced through his whole huge empire, every wife will respect her husband, whether he is important or not.”
The king and his princes liked this advice. So the king did what Memucan had said.

He sent letters to every province of his empire. Each letter was written in the alphabet of that province and the language of each people. The letters declared that each husband was master in his house and that his own language was to be spoken there.{i}

notes.text: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian name Xerxes. Xerxes I was king of Persia 486-465 BC. The Hebrew book of Esther never names God. The Greek form of Esther has six longer added passages; the CTB gives these with the Apocrypha. Cush was the land along the upper Nile River, in what is now Sudan.
Susa was the winter capital of the Persian kings, in what is now southwest Iran.
This was 483 BC.
This was about six months.
Some of these materials are not certain.
Vashti may mean “the one wanted” or “the best.”
Or “eunuchs.” The names in this book are Persian.
The Hebrew word for “crown” is a Persian word for a tall royal head covering.
The meaning of the last part is uncertain.

subheads.5: A Week of Feasting in Susa

verses.text: After a while, King Ahasuerus calmed down. Then his mind turned to Vashti, to her actions, and to the ruling made about her.
So his personal servants made a suggestion. “Let a search be made for beautiful young women who have never married,” they said. “They can be brought to the king.

Let the king choose men in every province of his empire to find all these lovely young women. Have them brought to the women’s quarters in the fortress city of Susa. Hegai, the king’s official in charge of the women, will look after them. Give them beauty treatments.{a}
Then let the young woman the king likes best become queen in Vashti’s place.” The plan pleased the king, and he put it into action.
Living in Susa’s fortress was a Jew whose name was Mordecai. He was from the tribe of Benjamin. His father was Jair, his grandfather was Shimei, and his great-grandfather was Kish.{b}
Kish had been taken from Jerusalem as a prisoner by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. He was taken with the group of captives that included Jeconiah, king of Judah.{c}

Mordecai was raising his uncle’s daughter, Hadassah, who was also known as Esther. She had lost both her father and her mother, so Mordecai had taken her in as his own daughter. She had a lovely figure and was beautiful to look at.{d}

When the king’s command and decree were made public, young women by the dozens were gathered into Susa’s fortress and handed over to Hegai. Esther was one of them. She was brought into the palace, where Hegai, keeper of the women, took charge of her.

Esther pleased Hegai, and he treated her with favor. Without delay he provided her beauty treatments and her share of food. From the palace he picked seven young women to be her maids. He moved her and her servants into the best rooms in the women’s quarters.
Esther had kept her people and her family a secret, as Mordecai had instructed her.
Mordecai paced in front of the women’s courtyard each day. He hoped to hear news of Esther and how she was being treated.

Each young woman had to complete a full year of beauty care before she was taken in to King Ahasuerus. For half a year she was rubbed with oil of myrrh. For the other half she was treated with perfumes and creams.
On the night a young woman went to the king, whatever she wanted to take along from the women’s quarters was given to her.

Evening was when she went in. When morning came, she was taken to a second house for women, run by Shaashgaz, the king’s official who watched over his wives. Unless the king was delighted with her and asked for her by name, she never saw him again.{e}

Then Esther’s turn came. She was the daughter of Abihail, who was Mordecai’s uncle, and Mordecai had raised her as his own child. When it was time for her to go in, she took only what Hegai, the king’s official in charge of the women, suggested. All who laid eyes on Esther thought well of her.
In the tenth month, called Tevet (in December–January), in the seventh year of King Ahasuerus’s reign, Esther was brought to him in the royal palace.{f}
Of all the women, Esther was the one the king loved most. No other young woman won so much of his favor and kindness. He set the royal crown on her head, and she became queen instead of Vashti.
Then the king held a great feast in Esther’s honor. He invited all his officials and servants. He gave the provinces a break from taxes and handed out gifts as only a king could.{g}
Later the young women were brought together once more. By then Mordecai held a post at the king’s gate.{h}
Esther kept her family and people secret, just as Mordecai had told her to. She kept on obeying Mordecai, just as she had when he was raising her.
During that time, while Mordecai sat at the king’s gate, two of the king’s officials became angry. They were Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the door. They made a plan to kill King Ahasuerus.
But Mordecai found out about it. He told Queen Esther, and she told the king, saying that Mordecai had discovered the plot.
The matter was looked into, and the report proved true. So the two officials were hung on a pole. All this was written down in the king’s presence in the book of the history of the kings.{i}

notes.text: Hegai is a Persian name. In verse 8 the Hebrew spells it Hege.
Mordecai is a Babylonian name, related to the name of the god Marduk.
This was in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10-17). The Hebrew may also mean that Mordecai himself was taken.
Hadassah means “myrtle.” Esther probably comes from a Persian word for “star.”
Shaashgaz is a Persian name.
This was at the end of 479 BC or the start of 478 BC, four years after Vashti lost her place (1:3).
Or “he declared a holiday.”
This means he served as an official at the royal court.
The Hebrew says “on a tree” or “on wood.” Probably they were put to death on a pointed pole. This is true all through the book.

subheads.8: Esther Is Taken to the Palace

verses.text: Later, King Ahasuerus honored Haman, son of Hammedatha, who was an Agagite. The king gave him a higher rank than any of the other princes.{a}
All the king’s officials at the king’s gate bowed down low to honor Haman, because the king had commanded it. Mordecai, however, refused to bend his knee or bow.
The other officials at the gate questioned him. “Why do you break the king’s command?”
They kept after him every day, yet he paid no attention. So they reported him to Haman. They wanted to see whether Haman would accept Mordecai’s reason, for Mordecai had told them he was a Jew.{b}
Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow or kneel to him, and he was filled with rage.

He thought it beneath him to punish only Mordecai. He had been told which people Mordecai belonged to. So Haman set out to wipe out every Jew in King Ahasuerus’s whole empire, since they were Mordecai’s people.

It was the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus. In the first month, the month of Nisan (in March–April), people cast Pur in front of Haman to choose a day and a month. Pur means “the lot.” The lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar (in February–March).{c}

Then Haman spoke to King Ahasuerus. “Spread out across all your provinces lives a people who keep to themselves,” he said. “Their laws are unlike those of any other nation. The king’s laws mean nothing to them. Letting them go on like this does the king no good.
If it pleases the king, let an order be sent out to destroy them. I will pay about 375 tons of silver to the king’s officials who carry out this work. It can go into the royal treasury.”{d}
So the king took off the ring he used to seal his orders. He gave it to Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
“Keep your money,” the king told Haman. “And do what you like with those people.”

On the thirteenth day of the first month, Haman called for the king’s writers. They wrote out everything Haman ordered. The letters went to the king’s regional rulers, to the governors of every province, and to the leaders of every people. Each province got its own script, and each people got its own language. They were written in King Ahasuerus’s name and sealed with his ring.{e}

Riders took the letters out to every province the king ruled. The order was to kill, wipe out, and destroy all the Jews, young and old, women and little children, all on a single day. That day was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar (in February–March). Their goods were to be taken as loot.{f}
A copy of the order was to be made law in every province. Every people was to hear it read, so they could prepare for the day.

The riders rushed off, sent by the king’s word. The order was also announced in the fortress city of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink. But all through the city of Susa, people were stunned and confused.

notes.text: Haman and Hammedatha are probably Persian names. “Agagite” reminds readers of Agag, king of Amalek, the enemy of Saul son of Kish (1 Samuel 15). Mordecai came from Kish’s family (2:5).
Some Hebrew copies spell the verb a little differently.
This was 474 BC. Pur is a Babylonian word for “lot.” Its plural, Purim, gives the festival its name (9:24-26). The Septuagint adds that the lot fell on the thirteenth day of Adar (see verse 13).
The Hebrew says “10,000 talents.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
This was the day before Passover (Leviticus 23:5).
This was eleven months later, in 473 BC.

verses.text: When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he ripped his clothes. He dressed in sackcloth, smeared ashes on himself, and walked out into the middle of the city wailing loudly and bitterly.
He went no farther than the space in front of the king’s gate. No one wearing sackcloth was allowed to pass through it.
In every province where the king’s command and law arrived, the Jews mourned deeply. They went without food, cried, and wailed. Sackcloth spread on ashes became the bed of many.

Esther’s young women and her officials came to tell her what was happening. The queen was terribly upset. She had fresh clothes sent out to Mordecai to wear in place of the sackcloth. He sent them back.
Then Esther summoned Hathach, an official the king had appointed to serve her. She sent him to Mordecai to find out what was troubling him and why.{a}
Hathach found Mordecai in the city’s open square, near the entrance to the king’s gate.
There Mordecai poured out the whole story. He named the exact sum of silver Haman had offered to pay into the royal treasury if the Jews were destroyed.{b}

He gave Hathach a copy of the law that had been announced in Susa, ordering their destruction. Hathach was to show it to Esther and explain it. Mordecai urged her to go before the king, ask him for mercy, and speak up on behalf of her own people.
Hathach returned and repeated Mordecai’s words to Esther.
Esther then sent Hathach back to Mordecai with this answer:

“Every official of the king and every person in his provinces understands this rule. If anyone, man or woman, enters the inner courtyard to see the king without being sent for, there is only one law: death. Only if the king stretches out his gold scepter toward that person will he live. And it has been thirty days since the king last called for me.”
Esther’s words were passed on to Mordecai.
Mordecai sent word back to Esther: “Don’t imagine that because you live in the palace, you will be the one Jew who escapes.

If you say nothing at a moment like this, the Jews will find help and rescue some other way. But you will perish, and so will your father’s family. And who can say? Maybe this very moment is the reason you were made queen.”{c}
Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai:

“Go and bring together all the Jews in Susa. Go without food for my sake. For three days and nights take no food or water. My young women and I will fast the same way. Then I will go in to the king, though the law forbids it. And if that costs me my life, so be it.”
So Mordecai left and did all that Esther had told him.

notes.text: Hathach is a Persian name.
Some Hebrew copies spell “the Jews” with an extra letter. The same is true at 8:1, 8:7, 8:13, 9:15, and 9:18.
Many readers have seen “somewhere else” as a hidden way of speaking about God, whom this book never names.

verses.text: Three days later, Esther put on her royal clothing. She took her place in the palace’s inner courtyard, across from the king’s hall. The king was seated on his throne inside the hall, facing the doorway.
He caught sight of Queen Esther standing in the courtyard, and he was pleased with her. He held out the gold scepter in his hand toward her. So Esther came near and touched the end of the scepter.
“What is it, Queen Esther?” the king asked her. “What would you like? I would give you anything, even up to half of my kingdom.”
Esther answered, “If it pleases the king, I would like you to come today, with Haman, to a meal I have made ready in your honor.”
“Hurry and fetch Haman,” the king said. “We will do as Esther asks.” So the two of them went to Esther’s banquet.
While the wine was being served, the king asked Esther again, “Now what is it you want? It will be given to you. What is your request? I will grant it, even up to half the kingdom.”
Esther replied, “Here is what I want and what I ask.

If the king looks on me with kindness, and if he is willing to give me my wish and grant my request, then please come again tomorrow, with Haman, to another banquet I will prepare. Then I will tell the king what I want.”

Haman left that day in high spirits, feeling wonderful. Then at the king’s gate his eyes fell on Mordecai. Mordecai did not stand up for him, and he showed no fear of him. Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.
But Haman kept control of himself and went on home. There he sent for his wife Zeresh and his friends to join him.{a}
Haman bragged to them that he owned so much and had so many sons. He went over every honor the king had given him. He said the king had raised him above the other officials and servants.
“And that’s not all,” Haman added. “When Queen Esther gave her banquet, the only guest she let come with the king was me. And she has invited me again tomorrow to eat with her and the king.
But I can take no joy in any of it while that Jew Mordecai keeps sitting there at the royal gate.”

His wife Zeresh and all his friends gave him an idea. “Build a pole 75 feet high,” they said. “Tomorrow morning, speak to the king and get his permission to hang Mordecai on it. After that, go off to the banquet with the king and have a good time.” Haman liked this idea, and he had the pole put up.{b}

notes.text: Zeresh is a Persian name.
The Hebrew says “50 cubits,” about 23 meters.

verses.text: That night the king could not sleep. He ordered that the record book of the important events of his reign be brought and read to him.
In it was written how Mordecai had warned about Bigthana and Teresh. They were two of the king’s officials who guarded the door, and they had planned to kill King Ahasuerus.
“What honor or reward did Mordecai get for this?” the king asked. His servants replied, “He has received nothing at all.”

“Who is in the courtyard?” the king asked. As it happened, Haman had just entered the palace’s outer courtyard. He had come to get the king’s approval to hang Mordecai on the pole that now stood waiting.
“It is Haman out there,” the servants answered. “Let him come in,” said the king.
Haman entered, and the king asked him, “If the king wishes to honor someone, how should it be done?” Haman said to himself, “Surely the king could only mean me!”
So Haman replied, “Here is what should be done for someone the king takes pleasure in honoring.
Have someone bring a royal robe, one the king himself has put on. Bring out a horse that the king rides, with a royal crest on its head.{a}

Then put the robe and the horse in the hands of one of the king’s most noble princes. Let him dress the man the king wants to honor. Let him lead the man on the horse through the city square. Have him call out before him, ‘See how the king treats someone he chooses to honor!’”
“Go at once,” the king told Haman. “The robe and horse you spoke of, get them now. Carry out every bit of it for Mordecai the Jew, who sits by the king’s gate. Leave out none of it.”

So Haman went and got the robe and the horse. He dressed Mordecai in the robe, set him on the horse, and led him through the city square. He called out before him, “See how the king treats someone he chooses to honor!”
Mordecai then returned to his place at the king’s gate. Haman, though, hurried home. His head was covered in grief and shame.

He told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened. His wise advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, “Your downfall has begun, and Mordecai is a Jew. If so, you cannot win against him. Your ruin before him is certain.”
They had not finished speaking when the king’s officials showed up. Quickly they took Haman off to Esther’s banquet.

notes.text: Old Persian carvings show royal horses wearing a crest. Or “and on whose head a royal crown has been put,” meaning the man.

verses.text: So the king came with Haman to the queen’s second banquet to share wine with her.
On this second day, as the wine was poured, the king once again put the question to Esther. “Queen Esther, tell me your wish, and I will give it. Name your request. Up to half my kingdom is yours.”
Queen Esther answered, “My king, if you look on me with kindness, and if it seems right to you, here is my wish: let me live. And here is my request: let my people live too.

Someone has sold us, me and my people, for slaughter and destruction, to be wiped out. Had we merely been sold into slavery, I would have held my tongue. That trouble would not be worth bothering the king about.”{a}
King Ahasuerus demanded of Queen Esther, “Who would dare do such a thing? Where is this man?”
Esther said, “The one who hates us, our enemy, is this wicked Haman!” Haman was struck with terror in front of the king and queen.
Furious, the king left his wine and stormed out to the palace garden. Haman remained in the room to plead with Queen Esther for his life. He knew the king’s mind was made up to bring disaster on him.

The king came back in from the garden to the banquet hall. Haman had just fallen onto the couch where Esther was reclining. “Will he even attack the queen right here in my palace, with me in the house?” the king shouted. As soon as the words were spoken, servants covered Haman’s face.

Harbonah, one of the officials serving the king, spoke up. “Look, there is a pole standing at Haman’s house, 75 feet tall. Haman set it up for Mordecai, the man whose warning saved the king.” “Hang Haman on it!” the king ordered.{b}
So Haman was hung on the very pole he had put up for Mordecai. Then the king’s anger died down.

notes.text: Or “for our enemy could never make up for the king’s loss.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew says “50 cubits,” about 23 meters.

verses.text: On that very day King Ahasuerus handed over to Queen Esther the house and property of Haman, the Jews’ enemy. Esther had explained to the king what Mordecai was to her, so Mordecai was brought before him.{a}
The signet ring that had once been on Haman’s finger was back with the king. Now he slipped it off and handed it to Mordecai. Esther made Mordecai manager over Haman’s whole estate.
Then Esther came to the king once more. She fell down at his feet, sobbing. She pleaded with him to undo the harm Haman the Agagite had planned, his scheme to destroy the Jews.
For a second time the king stretched the gold scepter out to her. Esther stood up before the king.

“My king,” she said, “if it pleases you, and if you look on me with favor, and if this seems right and proper to you, please write an order. If I please you, let it cancel the letters Haman wrote. Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, sent those letters to destroy the Jews in all the king’s provinces.
How could I bear to watch disaster fall on my people? How could I stand to see my own family destroyed?”
King Ahasuerus gave his reply to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew. “Haman’s estate now belongs to Esther,” he said. “And Haman has been hung on the pole for reaching out to strike the Jews.

Now you write another order for the Jews, whatever you think best. Write it in the king’s name and seal it with the king’s ring. No order written in the king’s name and sealed with his ring can ever be taken back.”

So the king’s writers were called in at once. It was the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan (in May–June). They wrote down all of Mordecai’s orders. The letters went to the Jews and to the regional rulers, governors, and officials of the 127 provinces from India to Cush. Each province received them in its own script, and each people in its own language. The Jews received them in their own script and language too.{b}
Mordecai wrote the letters in King Ahasuerus’s name and sealed them with the king’s ring. He sent them with messengers who rode fast horses, horses raised especially for the king’s service.{c}

The king’s order allowed the Jews, city by city, to band together and fight for their lives. They could destroy, kill, and wipe out any armed force from any people or province that attacked them, even its women and children. Their enemies’ goods could be taken as loot.{d}
This would happen on one day in all of King Ahasuerus’s provinces. That day was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar (in February–March).
Each province was to receive a copy of the order as its law. It was to be announced to every people. That way the Jews would be ready on that day to fight back against their enemies.{e}
Pushed on by the king’s command, the messengers raced off on the king’s fast horses. The order was also announced in the fortress city of Susa.
When Mordecai came out from seeing the king, he wore royal robes of blue and white. He wore a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. All over Susa, people cheered and celebrated.
Light had dawned for the Jews, bringing gladness, joy, and honor.

In every province and every city that the king’s command reached, the Jews were glad and full of joy. They held feasts and celebrated. Many people from other nations became Jews, because they were now afraid of the Jews.{f}

notes.text: For the spelling of “Jews” here and in verses 7 and 13, see the note at 4:7.
This was about two months after Haman’s order (3:12), in 474 BC.
The Hebrew words for these horses are Persian words. Their exact meaning is uncertain.
These words repeat Haman’s order (3:13). Some think “their women and children” means the Jews’ own families who were attacked.
Some Hebrew copies spell this word differently.
Or “pretended to be Jews.”

verses.text: The day came when the king’s command and law were to be carried out. It was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar (in February–March). The Jews’ enemies had been counting on that day to overpower them. But everything was turned upside down. Instead, the Jews crushed those who hated them.{a}
In their cities in every province of King Ahasuerus, the Jews came together to attack anyone who wanted to harm them. No one could stand up to them, because all the peoples were afraid of them.
Every official in the provinces helped the Jews, from the regional rulers and governors to those who managed the king’s business. They were all afraid of Mordecai.{b}
Mordecai had become powerful in the palace. His fame spread through every province, and his power kept growing.
With the sword the Jews cut down every enemy, killing and destroying them. Those who hated them got the treatment they had planned for the Jews.
In the fortress city of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men.
Among the dead were Parshandatha and Dalphon, and Aspatha,{c}
Poratha and Adalia, and Aridatha,
Parmashta and Arisai, and Aridai and Vaizatha.
All ten were sons of Haman, whose father was Hammedatha, and who had been the Jews’ great enemy. Yet the Jews kept their hands off the plunder.
That same day, the king was told how many had been killed in the fortress city of Susa.

He said to Queen Esther, “Just in the fortress of Susa, the Jews have killed and destroyed 500 men and Haman’s ten sons. Think what they must have done in the other provinces! Now what else do you want? You will have it. What more do you ask? It will be done.”
“If the king approves,” Esther replied, “let the Jews of Susa have one more day to act under today’s law. And let the bodies of Haman’s ten sons be hung on the pole.”{d}
So the king gave the order. A law was announced in Susa, and Haman’s ten sons were hung up.
On the fourteenth day of Adar, the Jews in Susa came together again. They killed 300 more men in Susa, but they took no loot.{e}

Meanwhile, the rest of the Jews in the king’s provinces had also come together to defend their lives. They won rest from their enemies. Those who hated them lost 75,000 men, yet the Jews took no plunder.{f}
All this took place on Adar’s thirteenth day. The next day, the fourteenth, they rested. It became a time of feasting and happiness.
But the Jews in Susa had come together on the thirteenth and fourteenth days. So they rested on the fifteenth day and made that a day of feasting and joy.
That is why Jews who live in country villages celebrate the fourteenth day of Adar. They make it a day of joy and feasting, a holiday, and a day for sending gifts of food to each other.{g}
Mordecai put all these events in writing. Then he sent letters to every Jew in each province of King Ahasuerus, whether near or far away.
His letters told them to keep both the fourteenth and the fifteenth of Adar as holidays, year after year.{h}

Those were the days when the Jews got rest from their enemies. In that month their grief was changed into gladness, and their mourning into a holiday. So they were to keep those days with feasting and joy. They were to send gifts of food to one another and give presents to the poor.
So the Jews agreed to keep on doing what they had started, following Mordecai’s written instructions.
Haman, Hammedatha’s son, the Agagite who hated all the Jews, had plotted to destroy them. He had cast the Pur, which means the lot, to crush and destroy them.{i}
But once the king learned of it, he gave written orders. Haman’s evil scheme against the Jews fell back on his own head. Both Haman and his sons ended up hanging on the pole.{j}
That is why these days are called Purim, from the word Pur. Mordecai’s letter had told them everything, and they had seen it all and lived through it themselves.{k}

So the Jews set up a lasting custom for themselves, their children, and everyone who joined them. They would never fail to celebrate these two days every year, in the way that was written and at the right time.{l}

These days would be remembered and celebrated in every generation, by every family, in every province and city. These days of Purim would never stop being kept among the Jews. Their children would never forget them.
Then Queen Esther, Abihail’s daughter, along with Mordecai the Jew, wrote a second letter about Purim. She used all her authority to make it official.
Letters were sent to all the Jews in the 127 provinces of Ahasuerus’s kingdom. They were words of peace and truth.

The letters set the days of Purim at their proper times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had ordered. The Jews had already accepted this for themselves and their children, along with times of fasting and mourning.{m}
Esther’s command made these rules about Purim official, and it was written down in the record.

notes.text: This was in 473 BC.

Today Purim is kept on the fourteenth of Adar. In Jerusalem and other cities that had walls in ancient times, it is kept on the fifteenth.
In our calendar these days fall in February or March.

The Fast of Esther is kept on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Purim.

verses.text: King Ahasuerus made the people of the mainland and of the far-off coasts pay him taxes.{a}

All his mighty deeds and powerful acts are written down. So is the full story of how great Mordecai became when the king raised him to high honor. You can read it all in the official records kept by the rulers of Media and Persia.

Only King Ahasuerus outranked Mordecai the Jew. He was a great man among the Jews, and his many relatives held him in high regard. He always looked out for his people’s good, and he spoke for the peace and safety of their children.
